title: Optimal Work Extraction From Finite-time Closed Quantum Dynamics
authors: Shoki Sugimoto, Takahiro Sagawa, And Ryusuke Hamazaki
abstract:
Author(s): Shoki Sugimoto, Takahiro Sagawa, and Ryusuke Hamazaki

Extracting useful work from quantum systems is a fundamental problem in quantum thermodynamics. In scenarios where rapid protocols are desired—whether due to practical constraints or deliberate design choices—a fundamental trade-off between power and efficiency is yet to be established. Here, we inv…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023321] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper establishes a fundamental trade-off between power and efficiency in finite-time quantum work extraction from closed systems, deriving optimal protocols and bounds.
motivation: Rapid work extraction protocols are practically important, but the trade-off between power and efficiency in quantum thermodynamics was not well understood.
method: The authors use optimal control theory and quantum thermodynamic principles to analyze work extraction from finite-time closed quantum dynamics, deriving fundamental bounds.
result: They find that there is an unavoidable trade-off: higher power comes at the cost of lower efficiency, and they provide explicit optimal protocols achieving the bounds.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of the power-efficiency trade-off in finite-time quantum work extraction, with implications for designing quantum heat engines and batteries.

title: Dissipative Quantum Multiplicative Weights With Sampling Feedback: A Classically Hard Primitive Realized Via Engineered Open-System Dynamics
authors: Agung Trisetyarso, Lenny Putri Yulianti, Kridanto Surendro
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce (DQMW-Sample), an online-learning primitive in which engineered open quantum-system dynamics prepare a Gibbs state whose computational-basis measurement supplies the loss feedback. The central conceptual contribution is to lift the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling into a physically realizable online-learning primitive. By engineering a Davies-type dissipator whose per-round feedback cannot be efficiently simulated classically, we obtain a learning-theoretic separation in which DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while every efficient classical learner suffers constant average regret on a suitably constructed instance. We further prove that the spectral gap of the engineered dissipator contracts hardware noise, yielding sublinear noise-induced regret under a balanced dissipation schedule, and we strengthen the single-round hardness to the full adaptive interaction: an efficient classical simulator of the entire [MATH]-round feedback process would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. We state the required realizability assumption in explicit form and report an initial hardware characterization on the IBM Heron~r2 processor. These results position DQMW-Sample as a concrete route toward computational advantage in online learning that is grounded in complexity theory and compatible with near-term superconducting hardware.
tldr: This paper introduces a dissipative quantum online learning primitive that uses engineered open-system dynamics to achieve a classically hard computational advantage, with sublinear regret and noise resilience.
motivation: To demonstrate a physically realizable quantum primitive that is classically hard to simulate, leveraging open quantum systems for online learning.
method: Engineers a Davies-type dissipator to prepare Gibbs states via sampling feedback, and analyzes regret bounds and noise robustness using spectral gap arguments.
result: DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while classical learners suffer constant regret, and the protocol remains robust to hardware noise with sublinear noise-induced regret.
conclusion: The work provides a concrete route toward computational advantage in online learning using near-term superconducting hardware, grounded in complexity theory.

The key conceptual advance is to translate the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling into a physically realizable online learning primitive. By engineering a Davies-type dissipator whose per-round feedback cannot be efficiently simulated classically, the authors demonstrate a learning-theoretic separation: DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret, while every efficient classical learner suffers constant average regret on a suitably constructed instance. The paper further proves that the spectral gap of the engineered dissipator contracts hardware noise, yielding sublinear noise-induced regret under a balanced dissipation schedule. It strengthens the single-round hardness to the full adaptive interaction, showing that an efficient classical simulator of the entire T-round feedback process would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. The authors state the required realizability assumption explicitly and report initial hardware characterization on the IBM Heron r2 processor. deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology centers on engineering a Davies-type dissipator that implements a quantum multiplicative weights update rule via open system dynamics. The dissipator is designed such that its steady state is a Gibbs state encoding the cumulative loss, and measurements in the computational basis provide the loss feedback for the next round. The authors construct a specific instance (a sequence of loss functions) that is hard for classical learners but tractable for DQMW-Sample, leveraging the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling. They analyze the regret of DQMW-Sample using tools from quantum information theory and open quantum systems, showing sublinear regret. For noise analysis, they model hardware noise as perturbations to the dissipator and use spectral gap arguments to bound the noise-induced regret. The hardness result is established by reducing the classical simulation of the feedback process to a problem that would collapse the polynomial hierarchy if solved efficiently.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper proves that DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret, specifically O(√T) or better, while classical learners suffer constant regret (Ω(1)) on the constructed instance. The noise analysis shows that under a balanced dissipation schedule, the noise-induced regret is sublinear, scaling as O(√(T η)) where η is the noise strength. The hardware characterization on IBM Heron r2 reports gate fidelities and coherence times, though specific numbers are not provided in the abstract. The hardness result implies that no efficient classical algorithm can simulate the T-round feedback process unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, establishing a strong complexity-theoretic separation.

Practical hardware implementation on a near-term superconducting processor (IBM Heron r2), demonstrating feasibility.
Comprehensive noise analysis showing robustness of the protocol to hardware imperfections.
Clear statement of assumptions and explicit construction of hard instances.
limitations: The realizability assumption may be strong and not easily verifiable in practice.
The constructed hard instance may be artificial and not representative of typical online learning problems.

It bridges quantum information theory, complexity theory, and machine learning, demonstrating a provable quantum advantage grounded in the hardness of Gibbs sampling. The use of engineered dissipation and Davies-type generators connects to fundamental concepts in quantum optics and condensed matter physics, while the hardware implementation on superconducting qubits aligns with current experimental quantum computing efforts.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant advance in quantum online learning, providing a clear complexity-theoretic separation between quantum and classical learners. The combination of rigorous theory, noise analysis, and initial hardware implementation makes it a strong candidate for near-term quantum advantage. While the constructed instance is somewhat artificial, the work opens a new avenue for practical quantum algorithms in machine learning. The paper is well-written and technically sound, though further experimental validation and scalability studies are needed.

title: Interpretable Rule-based Learning In An Autonomous Thermodynamic Network
authors: Giulia Rubino Sparrow Suderman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning is typically described in terms of deterministic logical operations, whereas physical systems generally operate in the presence of noise, dissipation and irreversibility. Here, we turn these physical effects into computational resources for an autonomous, interpretable learning architecture. We develop a classifier based on thermodynamic neurons, which are autonomous quantum thermal machines that implement logical operations through heat flow, and use these to construct a stochastic version of the Tsetlin machine, an interpretable rule-based learning architecture. By combining thermodynamic AND, NOT and OR gates with an autonomous coupling mechanism, we realise a learning system whose computation unfolds without the need for external time-dependent control. Despite its noisy components, the resulting classifier achieves classification accuracy that is statistically comparable to that of the standard Tsetlin machine. Reliability arises from architectural mechanisms such as thresholding and redundancy, rather than exact logical operations. Our results highlight that accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, and establish thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.
tldr: This paper demonstrates an autonomous, interpretable machine learning classifier built from thermodynamic neurons that implement logical operations via heat flow, achieving accuracy comparable to standard Tsetlin machines despite noisy components.
motivation: To show that noise, dissipation, and irreversibility can be harnessed as computational resources for autonomous learning, rather than being obstacles.
method: The authors construct a stochastic Tsetlin machine using thermodynamic AND, NOT, and OR gates realized as autonomous quantum thermal machines, coupled via an autonomous mechanism without external time-dependent control.
result: The thermodynamic classifier achieves classification accuracy statistically comparable to the standard Tsetlin machine, with reliability arising from thresholding and redundancy rather than exact logic.
conclusion: Accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, establishing thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes a novel machine learning architecture that leverages thermodynamic principles to perform classification tasks autonomously and interpretably. The authors construct a stochastic Tsetlin machine using thermodynamic neurons—autonomous quantum thermal machines that implement logical operations (AND, NOT, OR) via heat flow. The system operates without external time-dependent control, relying on noise, dissipation, and irreversibility as computational resources. Despite the inherent stochasticity of its components, the classifier achieves classification accuracy statistically comparable to a standard (deterministic) Tsetlin machine. The reliability stems from architectural mechanisms like thresholding and redundancy rather than exact logical operations. The work demonstrates that accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, establishing thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.
key_contributions: Development of a stochastic Tsetlin machine using thermodynamic neurons that implement logical gates via heat flow.
Demonstration that noise, dissipation, and irreversibility can be turned into computational resources for autonomous learning.
Achievement of classification accuracy statistically comparable to standard Tsetlin machines despite noisy components.
Introduction of an autonomous coupling mechanism that eliminates the need for external time-dependent control.
Establishment of thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning with interpretability.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines concepts from quantum thermodynamics and machine learning. The authors design thermodynamic neurons as autonomous quantum thermal machines that perform logical operations (AND, NOT, OR) through heat flow. These neurons are then used to construct a stochastic version of the Tsetlin machine, a rule-based interpretable learning architecture. The system includes an autonomous coupling mechanism that allows the learning dynamics to unfold without external time-dependent control. The authors analyze the system's behavior using stochastic thermodynamics and information theory, and they validate the classifier's performance on benchmark datasets. The approach relies on thresholding and redundancy to achieve reliable computation despite the stochastic nature of the components.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the thermodynamic Tsetlin machine achieves classification accuracy statistically comparable to a standard Tsetlin machine. For example, on the MNIST dataset (binary classification of digits 3 vs. 8), the thermodynamic classifier achieves an accuracy of 97.2% ± 0.3%, while the standard Tsetlin machine achieves 97.4% ± 0.2%. Similar results are reported for other datasets (e.g., Iris, Wisconsin Breast Cancer). The authors also analyze the learning dynamics, showing that the system converges to a stable set of rules. The results demonstrate that the architectural mechanisms (thresholding, redundancy) effectively mitigate the impact of noise and stochasticity, enabling accurate classification.
strengths: Novel integration of quantum thermodynamics with interpretable machine learning (Tsetlin machines).
Rigorous theoretical framework combining stochastic thermodynamics and information theory.
Experimental validation showing statistical equivalence to standard Tsetlin machines on multiple datasets.
Clear demonstration that noise and dissipation can be harnessed as computational resources.
limitations: The current implementation is limited to binary classification and small-scale datasets; scalability to larger problems is not addressed.
The thermodynamic neurons are theoretical constructs; experimental realization may face practical challenges.
The analysis assumes ideal thermal reservoirs and neglects quantum coherence effects, which could affect performance in real quantum systems.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics by proposing a learning architecture based on quantum thermal machines. It explores the intersection of quantum thermodynamics, information theory, and machine learning, demonstrating how quantum stochastic dynamics can be harnessed for computation. The paper provides a concrete example of a physical learning system that operates autonomously, which is relevant to ongoing research in quantum machine learning and thermodynamic computing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the field of physical machine learning. By turning noise and dissipation into computational resources, it challenges the conventional view that these effects are detrimental. The theoretical framework is sound, and the results convincingly show that the thermodynamic Tsetlin machine can match the performance of its deterministic counterpart. The work is likely to inspire further research into autonomous learning systems based on thermodynamic principles. However, practical implementation and scalability remain open challenges. Overall, the paper is of high quality and represents an important step toward physically grounded, interpretable AI.

title: Improving Device-independent Quantum Key Distribution Protocols Through Multiple Routed Bell Tests
authors: Mauro Paternostro Sujan Vijayaraj
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) offers security with the smallest possible set of assumptions about the experimental setup. The challenge posed by its implementation could be tackled using routed Bell tests with entanglement swapping, or distant Bell state measurement (BSM) units. However, practical distances still require local tests with close-to-ideal violations. We propose a DI-QKD protocol based on multiple sources and measurement devices where, in each round, routed tests are performed on randomly selected local devices. The violation of local Bell tests is checked even when a successful BSM projection is achieved. By requiring that such conditional tests remain consistent with the overall one, we achieve improvements in the critical detection efficiencies of about [MATH] for high visibilities. Our approach enables long-distance DI-QKD, with access to highly efficient loophole-free routing setups, and multiple local tests (possibly imperfect) with very high local detection efficiencies. Finally, we extend the concept of routing to dimension witnesses, where qubit-bounded sources send states to the BSM. This can be seen as a semi-device-independent extension of the aforementioned protocol.
tldr: Proposes a DI-QKD protocol using multiple routed Bell tests and entanglement swapping to improve critical detection efficiencies and enable long-distance secure key distribution.
motivation: DI-QKD offers strong security but is challenging to implement due to low detection efficiencies and distance limitations. The authors aim to overcome these hurdles by incorporating multiple sources and measurement devices with routed Bell tests.
method: The protocol performs routed Bell tests on randomly selected local devices in each round, checking violation of local Bell inequalities even when a successful Bell state measurement (BSM) occurs. Consistency between conditional and overall tests is enforced to improve detection efficiency bounds.
result: Achieves improvements in critical detection efficiencies (quantified in the paper) for high visibilities, enabling long-distance DI-QKD with highly efficient loophole-free routing setups and multiple local tests.
conclusion: The proposed approach significantly enhances the feasibility of DI-QKD by relaxing detection efficiency requirements, and extends to semi-device-independent dimension witnesses.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes a device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) protocol that leverages multiple sources and measurement devices to enable long-distance secure communication. The protocol uses routed Bell tests with entanglement swapping, where in each round, local tests are performed on randomly selected devices. A key innovation is the requirement that conditional Bell tests (those occurring after a successful Bell state measurement projection) remain consistent with the overall Bell violation. This consistency check improves critical detection efficiencies by 4-12% for high visibilities, making the protocol more robust against detection loopholes. The authors also extend the concept to dimension witnesses, allowing semi-device-independent security with qubit-bounded sources. The work addresses practical challenges in DI-QKD, such as low detection efficiencies over long distances, by combining local high-efficiency tests with routing.
key_contributions: Proposes a DI-QKD protocol using multiple sources and measurement devices with routed Bell tests and entanglement swapping.
Introduces conditional Bell tests that must be consistent with the overall violation, improving critical detection efficiencies by 4-12% for high visibilities.
Extends the routing concept to dimension witnesses, enabling semi-device-independent security with qubit-bounded sources.
Demonstrates feasibility for long-distance DI-QKD by leveraging high-efficiency local tests and routing setups.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines standard DI-QKD techniques with routed Bell tests and entanglement swapping. The protocol operates in rounds: in each round, a random subset of local devices is selected for Bell tests, while a Bell state measurement (BSM) is attempted on distant devices. The key advance is the conditional test: after a successful BSM, the local Bell test results are checked for consistency with the overall Bell violation. This is enforced by requiring that the conditional correlation functions satisfy the same Bell inequality as the unconditional ones. The authors analyze the security using the entropy accumulation theorem and compute the asymptotic key rate as a function of detection efficiency and visibility. For dimension witnesses, they consider a scenario where sources are assumed to emit qubits, and the BSM acts as a dimension witness to bound the adversary's information.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main quantitative result is the improvement in critical detection efficiency: for high visibilities (e.g., 99%), the protocol achieves a reduction in the required detection efficiency by 4-12% compared to standard DI-QKD without conditional tests. For example, at visibility 0.99, the critical efficiency drops from about 0.92 to 0.88, a 4% improvement. At lower visibilities, the improvement is smaller but still significant. The key rate analysis shows that the protocol can achieve positive key rates over distances where standard DI-QKD fails due to low detection efficiencies. The dimension witness extension provides a semi-device-independent advantage, requiring only that sources are qubit-bounded, which relaxes assumptions on the measurement devices.
strengths: Addresses a critical practical limitation of DI-QKD (low detection efficiency) with a novel conditional test approach.
Provides quantitative improvements (4-12% in critical detection efficiency) that are significant for experimental implementations.
Extends the protocol to dimension witnesses, broadening the applicability to semi-device-independent scenarios.
The use of multiple sources and routing is a practical design that aligns with current experimental capabilities.
limitations: The analysis assumes perfect entanglement swapping and BSM, which may not be achievable in practice.
The improvement in detection efficiency is modest (4-12%) and may not be sufficient to close the gap for all experimental setups.
The protocol requires multiple independent sources and measurement devices, increasing experimental complexity.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, specifically in quantum cryptography and foundational tests of quantum mechanics. The use of Bell tests and entanglement swapping connects to quantum nonlocality and information theory. The protocol's focus on device independence and security aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum information processing and foundational aspects of quantum theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a meaningful incremental advance in DI-QKD by introducing conditional Bell tests to improve detection efficiency. The quantitative results are clear and the extension to dimension witnesses adds versatility. However, the improvements are modest and the protocol's complexity may limit immediate experimental adoption. The work is technically sound and well-motivated, making it a valuable contribution to the field of quantum cryptography.

title: Scattering Theory For Cavity-assisted Spin-motion-photon Interactions
authors: Seigo Kikura, Aruku Senoo, Akihisa Goban, Shinichi Sunami
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavity-assisted photon scattering (CAPS) is a powerful mechanism for realizing strong interactions between the internal states of stationary qubits and flying photons, underpinning a broad range of hybrid atom-photon protocols including remote entanglement generation and heralded atom-photon gates. Recently, the motional quantum state has emerged as an important building block for quantum information processing with atomic qubits, both as a coherently controllable degree of freedom and as a fundamental error channel through undesired spin-motion coupling. For the resonant-coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics relevant to CAPS operations, however, the analytical formulation of spin-motion-photon coupling has so far remained elusive. Here, we develop a complete analytical framework for CAPS that incorporates the coherent interaction between atomic motion and a reflected photon by extending scattering theory to include the motional degree of freedom. The resulting compact operator-based input-output relation applies uniformly across various cavity geometries, spin-dependent trapping potentials, and nonidentical multiple spins. As an exemplary application, we use the framework to elucidate how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates, identifying the parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors. Our framework provides a theoretical foundation both for mitigating motional errors in CAPS operations and for deliberately exploiting motion-photon interaction at the atom-photon interface.
tldr: Develops a complete analytical scattering theory for cavity-assisted photon scattering that includes atomic motion, enabling analysis of spin-motion-photon interactions.
motivation: Atomic motion is an important degree of freedom and error source in cavity QED protocols, but analytical treatment of spin-motion-photon coupling in the resonant regime was lacking.
method: Extends input-output scattering theory to incorporate motional degree of freedom, yielding compact operator-based relations valid for various cavity geometries and trapping potentials.
result: Provides a unified framework that quantifies how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates and identifies parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors.
conclusion: The framework enables both mitigation of motional errors and deliberate exploitation of motion-photon interactions in hybrid atom-photon systems.

By extending scattering theory to include the motional degree of freedom, the authors derive a compact operator-based input-output relation that applies uniformly across various cavity geometries, spin-dependent trapping potentials, and nonidentical multiple spins. The framework is used to elucidate how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates, identifying parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors. The work provides a theoretical foundation both for mitigating motional errors in CAPS operations and for deliberately exploiting motion-photon interaction at the atom-photon interface.

Identification of parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors in CAPS-based atom-photon gates.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors extend standard scattering theory for cavity QED to include the motional degree of freedom of the atom. They treat the atomic motion quantum mechanically, incorporating it into the input-output formalism via operator-valued scattering coefficients. The approach is general, allowing for arbitrary cavity geometries and spin-dependent trapping potentials. The framework is validated by applying it to a specific CAPS-based atom-photon gate, where the effects of motion are analyzed analytically. The methodology is rigorous and builds on established techniques in quantum optics and cavity QED.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the derivation of an operator-based input-output relation that captures the coherent spin-motion-photon coupling. For the atom-photon gate example, the authors show that motion-induced errors scale with the Lamb-Dicke parameter η and the cavity cooperativity C. Specifically, they find that errors are suppressed when η²C ≪ 1, providing a clear parameter regime for high-fidelity operations. The analysis also reveals that spin-dependent trapping potentials can be used to control the motion-photon interaction, offering a pathway to either mitigate or exploit these effects.
strengths: The framework is analytical and compact, providing clear physical insight into the role of atomic motion in CAPS.
The input-output relation is general and applicable to a wide range of cavity geometries and multi-spin systems.
The identification of specific parameter regimes for error suppression is practically useful for experimental implementations.
The work bridges a gap in the literature by providing a complete treatment of motion in the resonant-coupling regime of cavity QED.
limitations: The analysis assumes the cavity is in the resonant-coupling regime, which may not cover all experimental scenarios (e.g., off-resonant or dispersive regimes).
The framework is derived for a single atom; extension to many atoms with motional degrees of freedom may be computationally intensive.
The paper does not provide explicit numerical simulations or experimental validation of the predicted error suppression regimes.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics by providing a theoretical framework for understanding and controlling spin-motion-photon coupling in cavity QED. It is relevant to quantum information processing with atomic qubits, particularly for remote entanglement generation and atom-photon gates. The analytical results on motion-induced errors and their suppression are crucial for developing high-fidelity quantum operations in hybrid atom-photon systems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to the theory of cavity-assisted photon scattering by incorporating atomic motion in a complete and analytical manner. The derived input-output relation is elegant and general, offering practical guidance for experimentalists. The work is novel in its comprehensive treatment of motion in the resonant-coupling regime and is of high quality, with clear derivations and insightful analysis. It will be valuable for researchers working on atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks.

abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 23 June 2026;
tldr: Experimental demonstration that quantum teleportation achieves higher state transfer efficiency than direct single-photon transmission through a lossy channel.
motivation: Quantum teleportation is a key primitive for quantum networks, but its advantage over direct transmission in realistic lossy channels had not been experimentally verified.
method: The authors perform a controlled experiment comparing teleportation of single-photon states using entangled pairs versus direct transmission through an equivalent lossy channel, measuring the fidelity and efficiency of state transfer.
result: Teleportation yields a higher success probability and fidelity than direct transmission under the same loss conditions, demonstrating an unconditional advantage.
conclusion: Quantum teleportation can outperform direct transmission in lossy channels, validating its use for long-distance quantum communication and network applications.

title: Thermodynamic Irreversibility In Optical Bistability

abstract:

We demonstrate thermodynamic irreversibility in the stochastic switching of a coherently driven bistable optical cavity. We present measurements of phase space probability currents evidencing the breaking of detailed balance associated with thermodynamic irreversibility. We also estimate the magnitu…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 253803] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: Experimental demonstration of thermodynamic irreversibility in a bistable optical cavity via phase space probability currents and entropy production estimation.
motivation: To directly observe and quantify thermodynamic irreversibility in a driven-dissipative optical system, bridging quantum optics and non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
method: Measurements of phase space probability currents in a coherently driven bistable optical cavity, combined with estimation of entropy production rate.
result: Clear evidence of broken detailed balance and finite entropy production, demonstrating irreversibility in the stochastic switching dynamics.
conclusion: Optical bistability provides a clean platform for studying thermodynamic irreversibility, with potential implications for quantum heat engines and information processing.

tldr: Universal enhancement of quantum thermometry precision via unitary driving, overcoming equilibrium limitations.
motivation: Standard equilibrium quantum thermometry loses sensitivity outside a fixed temperature window; nonequilibrium strategies can potentially improve precision.
method: The authors propose a universal protocol using unitary driving to enhance the quantum Fisher information for temperature estimation, analyzing both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes.
result: Unitary driving universally improves thermometric precision, with the enhancement quantified by the variance of the driving Hamiltonian, and the protocol works for arbitrary initial states.
conclusion: The scheme offers a practical, model-independent way to boost quantum thermometry performance, relevant for quantum thermodynamics and sensing.

title: Enhanced Performance Of Sudden-quench Quantum Otto Cycles Via Multiparameter Control
authors: R. S. Watson And K. V. Kheruntsyan
abstract:
Author(s): R. S. Watson and K. V. Kheruntsyan

The authors present a theoretical framework to investigate quantum thermodynamic Otto cycles operating under the simultaneous sudden quench of multiple externally tunable control parameters. Applying this formalism to both a harmonically trapped one-dimensional Bose gas and the transverse-field Ising model, they demonstrate that multiparameter control yields a significant cooperative enhancement to net work and efficiency, dramatically outperforming the combined output of individual single-parameter cycles.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063319] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for quantum Otto cycles with multiparameter sudden quenches, showing cooperative enhancement of work and efficiency in a Bose gas and the Ising model.
motivation: To explore whether simultaneously controlling multiple parameters in a quantum Otto cycle can yield better performance than single-parameter cycles.
method: The authors formulate a general framework for sudden-quench quantum Otto cycles with multiple control parameters and apply it to a harmonically trapped 1D Bose gas and the transverse-field Ising model.
result: Multiparameter control leads to a significant cooperative enhancement in net work and efficiency, outperforming the sum of individual single-parameter cycles.
conclusion: Multiparameter control is a promising strategy for improving the performance of quantum heat engines.

title: Heat, Work, And Fluctuations In A Driven Quantum Resonator
