title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has seen rapid progress since 2016.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical results on 2D magnetic materials, including topology, dynamics, and light-matter interactions.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topological phases, nonequilibrium dynamics, and potential applications.
conclusion: 2D van der Waals magnets offer a rich platform for fundamental physics and future technologies.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from condensed matter physics.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism, and electronic nematicity.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and topological phenomena.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses serve as a model system for complex disordered systems, and understanding their dynamics is relevant to many areas of physics.
method: The paper reviews experimental techniques, theoretical models, and large-scale numerical simulations of spin-glass dynamics.
result: The review highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation, and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with ongoing challenges and cross-disciplinary impact.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on material candidates and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: Review of theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental candidate materials, summarizing key properties and challenges.
result: Highlights leading candidate materials and their topological properties such as chiral edge modes.
conclusion: The review serves as a resource for researchers working on quantum spin liquids, but does not present new results or directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data, but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a key goal in neuroscience, and statistical physics offers tools to model such systems.
method: The review surveys maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques applied to recordings from thousands of neurons.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural populations, bridging theory and experiment.
conclusion: Statistical physics principles can provide predictive power for neural network dynamics, similar to their role in other areas of physics.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering their formation and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of magnetic skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum effects in skyrmions, including quantum tunneling and entanglement.
conclusion: Quantum properties of skyrmions are an emerging area with potential for future quantum technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects and entanglement mediation.
motivation: To understand the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, which is poorly understood, by using massive quantum systems as probes.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental efforts, including matter-wave interferometry, optomechanics, and tests of gravity-induced entanglement.
result: Summarizes current theoretical models and experimental progress, highlighting that no definitive evidence of quantum gravity has been found yet.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity, but further theoretical and experimental work is needed.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library (PyOpticL) for modular optical system design and demonstrates its use for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Conventional optical design is piecewise and not scalable, hindering quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a code-to-CAD tool using beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, and creates modular baseplates for common AMO subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates.
conclusion: Enables scalable, modular optical systems for quantum computing and other AMO experiments.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies electron trajectories in strong field ionization using squeezed light, focusing on quantum statistics effects on ultrafast dynamics.
motivation: To understand how squeezed light modifies electron dynamics in strong field ionization, potentially offering new control over ultrafast processes.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte-Carlo technique to simulate strong field ionization by squeezed states of light.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum distribution shows varying rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light provides additional control over ultrafast electron dynamics, but the atomic potential plays a crucial role.

title: Experimental Exclusion Of A Generalized Károlyházy Gravity-induced Decoherence Model
authors: Nicola Bortolotti, Kristian Piscicchia, Alessio Porcelli, Matthias Laubenstein, Simone Manti, Antonino Marcianò, Federico Nola And Catalina Curceanu
abstract: We report new experimental constraints on the generalized version of the gravity-induced decoherence model originally proposed by Károlyházy. Using data collected by the VIP Collaboration at the INFN Gran Sasso National Laboratory with a high-purity germanium detector, we derive an improved lower bound on the spatial correlation length characterizing metric fluctuations in the model. We obtain a bound m (95% C.L.), which exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the previous experimental limit. When combined with the theoretical upper bound m derived from macroscopic localization requirements, our result excludes the generalized Károlyházy model. The same conclusion applies to an associated non-Markovian formulation of the continuous spontaneous localization model. Our findings significantly tighten experimental constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios and demonstrate the sensitivity of underground low-background experiments to foundational modifications of quantum mechanics.
tldr: Experimental exclusion of a gravity-induced decoherence model using underground detector data.
motivation: To test foundational modifications of quantum mechanics that predict gravity-induced decoherence, which could affect quantum coherence in large systems.
method: Analysis of high-purity germanium detector data from the VIP Collaboration at Gran Sasso, deriving bounds on the spatial correlation length of metric fluctuations.
result: Improved lower bound on the correlation length by over an order of magnitude, excluding the generalized Károlyházy model when combined with theoretical upper bounds.
conclusion: The generalized Károlyházy gravity-induced decoherence model is ruled out, tightening constraints on gravity-related decoherence scenarios.

title: Random-with-constraints: Constructing Minimal Models For High-dimensional Biology
authors: Ilya Nemenmanpankaj Mehtaahttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Physics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322bhttps://ror.org/03czfpz43department Of Biology, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322chttps://ror.org/03czfpz43initiative In Theory And Modeling Of Living Systems, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322dhttps://ror.org/05qwgg493department Of Physics, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215ehttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing And Data Science, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
Biologists and physicists have a rich tradition of modeling dynamics of living systems with simple models composed of a few interacting components. Despite the remarkable success of this approach, it remains unclear how to use such finely tuned models to ...
tldr: This paper proposes a method for constructing minimal models of high-dimensional biological systems using random constraints.
motivation: Biologists and physicists often use simple models for complex systems, but it is unclear how to systematically build such models from data.
method: The authors introduce a 'random-with-constraints' framework that generates minimal models by imposing random constraints on model parameters.
result: The approach is demonstrated on biological examples, showing that it can capture essential dynamics while remaining interpretable.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to construct minimal models for high-dimensional biological systems, bridging data-driven and theory-driven approaches.

title: Estimating The Amount Of Computation Done By A Brain Using Population Neural Activity
authors: Junang Liyuzheng Linanuj Kumar Sharmaandrew M. Leiferdavid H. Wolpertahttps://ror.org/00hx57361department Of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544bhttps://ror.org/00hx57361princeton Neuroscience Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540chttps://ror.org/01arysc35santa Fe Institute, Santa Fe, NM 87501dinternational Center For Theoretical Physics, Trieste I-34151, Italyehttps://ror.org/023dz9m50complexity Science Hub, Vienna 1080, Austriafhttps://ror.org/03efmqc40arizona State University, Tempe, AZ 85287
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 25, June 2026.
SignificanceQuantifying the “amount of computation” a dynamic system performs is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes like neural activity. We introduce a broadly applicable data-driven framework defining the “amount of ...
tldr: This paper introduces a data-driven framework to estimate the amount of computation performed by a brain based on population neural activity.
motivation: Quantifying computation in dynamic systems like the brain is crucial for linking theoretical computer science to real-world processes.
method: The authors develop a framework that uses population neural activity data to define and estimate the 'amount of computation'.
result: The framework provides a way to measure computation in neural systems, with potential applications in neuroscience and complex systems.
conclusion: The work offers a novel approach to bridging computation theory and neural dynamics, but is not directly aligned with the user's research interests.

title: On Support Cardinality For Discrete Schr\"odinger Equation
authors: Linjun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How sparse can a nontrivial solution of a discrete Schr\"odinger equation be? In this note we study Dirichlet solutions on a finite [MATH]-dimensional lattice box, allowing an arbitrary real potential, and measure sparsity by the number of lattice sites at which the solution is nonzero (assuming it is nonzero at the origin). Our main result is a dimension-reduction principle: the minimal possible support size cannot decrease when the dimension increases. Consequently, any lower bound proved in dimension [MATH] automatically yields the same lower bound in dimension [MATH]. As an application, we obtain a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions, matching the best-known two-dimensional constructions up to a logarithmic factor.
tldr: This paper studies the minimal support size of nontrivial solutions to the discrete Schrödinger equation on a finite lattice, proving a dimension-reduction principle and obtaining a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions.
motivation: Understanding how sparse solutions can be for discrete Schrödinger equations is a fundamental mathematical question with potential implications for quantum mechanics and condensed matter physics, but the paper is purely mathematical.
method: The authors analyze Dirichlet solutions on a finite d-dimensional lattice box with an arbitrary real potential, using combinatorial and analytic arguments to prove a dimension-reduction principle.
result: The main result is that the minimal possible support size cannot decrease when dimension increases, and they obtain a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions matching best-known 2D constructions up to a logarithmic factor.
conclusion: The work provides a general lower bound technique for support cardinality, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Routes To Chaos In Class-B Laser Dimer Necklaces
authors: J. Diaz-Avila, A. A. Macias Infante, B. R. Jaramillo-Avila, B. M. Rodriguez-Lara
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear [MATH]-symmetric dimer necklaces use cyclic coupling to organize phase-locked modes, while class-B laser--resonator dimers use carrier inversion to destabilize gain--loss dynamics and produce routes to chaos. We study a cyclic necklace of class-B laser--resonator dimers to determine how inter-dimer coupling and cyclic phase constraints modify carrier-mediated instabilities. The carrier inversion turns the necklace into an amplitude--phase--carrier system whose active-site gain controls intensities, while the linewidth-enhancement factor shifts phases. We derive the real dynamical equations, identify uniform fixed points above threshold, and classify their phase configurations under cyclic closure. Even necklaces support full synchronization, a uniform [MATH] shift, and two alternating phase configurations; odd necklaces support only the first two. Linear stability of these configurations partitions the coupling plane into sixteen possible regions, including one region with no stable uniform fixed point. Long-time simulations for representative two- and three-dimer necklaces show stable lasing, multistability, and irregular lasing controlled by pump ratio and coupling strengths. Increasing the pump ratio expands stable domains and suppresses the region without stable uniform fixed points.
tldr: This paper studies chaos and synchronization in a necklace of class-B laser dimers, focusing on nonlinear dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how inter-dimer coupling and cyclic phase constraints modify carrier-mediated instabilities in laser arrays.
method: Derives real dynamical equations for the amplitude-phase-carrier system, identifies uniform fixed points, performs linear stability analysis, and runs long-time simulations.
result: Classifies sixteen stability regions in the coupling plane; even necklaces support four phase configurations while odd necklaces support two; increasing pump ratio stabilizes dynamics.
conclusion: The system exhibits stable lasing, multistability, and irregular lasing depending on pump and coupling parameters, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Giant Second-Harmonic Generation In 3R-MoS2/MLM Hybrid Metasurfaces Cavities
authors: Omar A. M. Abdelraouf
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear 2D materials such as 3R-phase molybdenum disulfide (3R-MoS2) offer strong second-order optical nonlinearities in an atomically thin platform, making them attractive for on-chip frequency conversion, quantum light generation, and integrated nonlinear nanophotonics. However, the second harmonic generation (SHG) efficiency of monolayer or few-layer 3R-MoS2 deposited on planar substrates remains fundamentally limited by weak light-matter interaction, poor phase matching, and small interaction volumes. Here, we introduce NanoPhotoNet-PINL, a physics informed AI-driven inverse design framework based on a hybrid one-dimensional convolutional neural network and deep neural network autoencoder, tailored for nonlinear MLMs metasurfaces. The model directly maps target dual-resonant reflection spectra at the fundamental and second-harmonic wavelengths to the required multi-layer geometries and material compositions that maximize the effective nonlinear overlap with an embedded 3R-MoS2 sheet. By integrating Maxwell-based nonlinear electrodynamics into the inverse design loop, we compute the second-harmonic conversion efficiency and modal overlap factors for each predicted MLMs design, enabling physics-guided training and evaluation. Our approach achieves an inverse-design prediction efficiency exceeding ~99.2 % along the linear spectral manifold, while the optimized dual-resonant MLMs yield more than three orders of magnitude enhancement in SHG intensity compared to a bare 3R-MoS2 flake on a planar substrate. NanoPhotoNet-PINL establishes a generalizable paradigm for intelligent inverse design of nonlinear multi-layer metasurfaces and phase-matched dual-resonant cavities for high-efficiency second-order processes.
tldr: This paper uses a physics-informed neural network to inversely design nonlinear metasurfaces for enhanced second-harmonic generation in 3R-MoS2.
motivation: Second-harmonic generation efficiency in atomically thin 3R-MoS2 is limited by weak light-matter interaction and poor phase matching; the authors aim to overcome this via optimized metasurface cavities.
method: A hybrid CNN-autoencoder (NanoPhotoNet-PINL) is trained to map target dual-resonant reflection spectra to multilayer geometries, with Maxwell-based nonlinear electrodynamics integrated into the inverse design loop.
result: The inverse design achieves >99.2% prediction efficiency along the linear spectral manifold, and optimized dual-resonant metasurfaces yield over 1000× enhancement in SHG intensity compared to bare 3R-MoS2 on a planar substrate.
conclusion: The framework provides a generalizable paradigm for intelligent inverse design of nonlinear multilayer metasurfaces for high-efficiency second-order processes.

title: Low-Threshold Degenerate Optical Parametric Oscillations In Bichromatically-Pumped Normal-Dispersion Photonic-Crystal Microresonator
authors: Valery E. Lobanov, Nadezhda S. Tatarinova, Artem E. Shitikov, Olga V. Borovkova, Igor A. Bilenko, Dmitry A. Chermoshentsev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The process of excitation of degenerate optical parametric oscillations via bichromatic pump is studied numerically in normal-dispersion photonic-crystal microresonator. It is demonstrated that the photonic-crystal structure with two split modes placed symmetrically at the particular interval from the pumped modes provides significant reduction in pump power threshold for the considered process. The parameter range for this phenomenon is determined. Introduction of mode splitting at the signal mode located in the center between pumped modes leads to an increase in the generation threshold.
tldr: This paper studies degenerate optical parametric oscillations in a photonic-crystal microresonator with bichromatic pumping, focusing on threshold reduction.
motivation: To achieve low-threshold parametric oscillations in normal-dispersion microresonators for applications in frequency comb generation and nonlinear optics.
method: Numerical simulation of a photonic-crystal microresonator with split modes, analyzing pump power thresholds for degenerate optical parametric oscillation under bichromatic pumping.
result: Bichromatic pumping with symmetrically placed split modes significantly reduces the pump power threshold, while splitting at the signal mode increases it.
conclusion: The proposed photonic-crystal design enables low-threshold parametric oscillations, which may benefit integrated photonic devices.

title: Wave-Particle Decomposition For Kinetic Equations I: Theory And Numerics
authors: Kun Xu Chang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a wave-particle decomposition (WPD) for kinetic relaxation equations, formulated around a local evolution timescale and its associated kinetic horizon. By leveraging the characteristic integral solution, we decompose the distribution function into an analytically accumulated wave component and a purely kinetic particle component. The latter is defined by the collisionless transport that survives beyond a prescribed local domain of influence, termed the horizon. This continuous formulation yields a unified wave-particle system valid across the entire Knudsen spectrum, comprising a source-free total conservation law, a wave equation, and a particle equation. The wave operator admits a Chapman--Enskog expansion, whose moments yield Euler and Navier--Stokes fluxes with horizon-dependent coefficients, while the particle equation governs the remaining non-equilibrium kinetic transport. At the algorithmic level, this system is discretized by a conservative macro-micro method. The total conservative variables are advanced by a finite-volume update using the sum of a Navier--Stokes gas-kinetic wave flux and a particle flux computed by either a deterministic discrete-ordinate [MATH] method or a Monte Carlo representation. Unlike the global time-step splitting in the unified gas-kinetic wave-particle (UGKWP) method, the present partition is defined at the PDE level and governed by the local ratio of evolution timescale to relaxation time. The particle component is therefore a fractional kinetic population generated by the collisionless factor of the integral solution. Formal analysis establishes the asymptotic-preserving continuum limit, rarefied-regime consistency, and regime-adaptive scaling of active kinetic degrees of freedom. Numerical tests in one, two, and three dimensions validate the accuracy, multiscale capability, and efficiency of the framework.
tldr: This paper introduces a wave-particle decomposition for kinetic equations, unifying continuum and rarefied gas dynamics across all Knudsen numbers.
motivation: To develop a unified framework that bridges continuum and kinetic regimes without global time-step splitting, improving multiscale simulation efficiency.
method: The distribution function is decomposed into an analytically accumulated wave component and a kinetic particle component based on a local horizon; the system is discretized via a conservative macro-micro finite-volume method.
result: The method is asymptotic-preserving, regime-adaptive, and validated in 1D, 2D, and 3D tests, showing accuracy and efficiency across the Knudsen spectrum.
conclusion: The wave-particle decomposition provides a PDE-level partition that naturally adapts to local rarefaction, offering a promising approach for multiscale kinetic simulations.

title: On The Simple Derivation Of The Casimir Effect
authors: Matthias Kleinmann Hai-Chau Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Casimir effect in its simplest form describes the attraction of two parallel conducting plates at close distance due to the vacuum fluctuation of the electromagnetic field. Its derivation can be found in many introductory works on quantum optics. Here we return to the original paper by Casimir and find subtle nuances in his derivation that are worth discussing to give a complete picture of a mathematically sound derivation of the effect.
tldr: The paper revisits Casimir's original derivation of the Casimir effect, discussing mathematical nuances for a sound derivation.
motivation: To clarify subtle points in Casimir's original derivation that are often glossed over in textbooks.
method: The authors analyze Casimir's original paper step-by-step, identifying and addressing mathematical gaps.
result: A mathematically rigorous derivation of the Casimir effect is presented, with careful handling of regularization and boundary conditions.
conclusion: The Casimir effect derivation can be made fully rigorous by addressing subtle mathematical issues, confirming the physical result.

title: Refractive Indices Of Y$_2$SiO$_5$ In The Near-infrared
authors: Shijun Zhang, J\'er\^ome Debray, Beno\^it Boulanger, Pierre Lemonde, Thierry Chaneli\`ere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Y[MATH]SiO[MATH] is a reference birefringent material for optical quantum technologies. The refractive index is primarily known in the visible spectrum, whereas this crystal is also used in the near-infrared. We begin by analysing historical measurements, as well as the modelling proposed at the time. The absence of refractive index tabulated values in the near- and mid-infrared ranges motivated us to carry out independent measurements. Using interferometric techniques in the telecom wavelength range, we demonstrate the ability to determine the principal refractive indices and propose a model spanning a broad spectral range based on Sellmeier equations for which we explicitly give the coefficients and discuss the achievable accuracy. Conversely, as an illustration, white-light interference enables us to precisely determine the thickness of a Y[MATH]SiO[MATH] thin film on the order of ten micrometers.
tldr: This paper measures and models the refractive indices of Y2SiO5 in the near-infrared using interferometric techniques.
motivation: Y2SiO5 is a key material for optical quantum technologies, but its refractive index data in the near-infrared is lacking.
method: Interferometric measurements in the telecom wavelength range are performed to determine principal refractive indices, and Sellmeier equations are fitted to model the dispersion.
result: Accurate refractive index values and a Sellmeier model covering a broad spectral range are provided, with explicit coefficients and accuracy estimates.
conclusion: The results enable precise thickness determination of Y2SiO5 thin films and support applications in quantum optics.

title: Temporal Wave Trapping From Dynamical Pump Pulses
authors: T. Torres, R. Terrier, J. Fatome, B. Kibler, G. Millot, G. P. Agrawal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal reflection in nonlinear optical fibers provides a powerful framework for manipulatinglight. In this work, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate a novel mechanism for wavetrapping induced by the dynamical evolution of a single high-order soliton pulse. Experimentalmeasurements performed in a 5-km-long nonlinear dispersion shifted fiber confirm the coexistence ofreflected, transmitted, and trapped components, in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions.These results establish a simple and versatile route toward dynamic temporal waveguiding using asingle optical pulse, opening new opportunities for all-optical control and manipulation of ultrafastsignals.
tldr: Demonstrates temporal wave trapping via dynamical pump pulses in nonlinear optical fibers.
motivation: To achieve all-optical control and manipulation of ultrafast signals using a simple single-pulse mechanism.
method: Theoretical modeling and experimental measurements in a 5-km nonlinear dispersion-shifted fiber with high-order soliton pulses.
result: Coexistence of reflected, transmitted, and trapped components observed, matching theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Establishes a versatile route for dynamic temporal waveguiding with potential applications in all-optical signal processing.

title: In-plane Vector-field Imaging Of Propagating Surface Phonon Polaritons
authors: Richarda Niemann, Doroth\'ee S. Mader, Gonzalo Alvarez-P\'erez, Ana I. F. Tresguerres-Mata, Aitana Tarazaga Mart\'in-Luengo, Stefan Partel, Joshua D. Caldwell, Niclas S. Mueller, Martin Wolf, Javier Mart\'in-S\'anchez, Pablo Alonso-Gonz\'alez, Alexander Paarmann
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polariton interferometry through optical near-field microscopy has become a powerful tool in nanophotonics, enabling direct spatial access to the propagation characteristics of strongly confined, evanescent polariton modes. Scattering-type near-field optical microscopy has matured as the prime tool for such studies, yet mostly the out-of-plane components of the optical near fields are probed, owing to the elongated geometry of the nanotip. Here, we demonstrate a complementary far-field nonlinear microscopy approach which allows to selectively probe in-plane polariton field components. Accessing the full vector field is interesting when studying complex mode patterns such as hyperbolic polaritons or skyrmions, where the in-plane field components are typically only inferred from the out-of-plane component but not measured directly. To this end, we use nonlinear infrared-visible wide-field sum-frequency generation microscopy, where the short visible wavelength of the nonlinear signal provides the high spatial resolution to access evanescent modes in the infrared. The symmetry selection rules of the nonlinear process further enable polarization-selective imaging of both in-plane polariton field components through spatial interferometry. The concept is demonstrated experimentally using surface phonon polaritons at the AlN-air interface launched by a gold antenna. A simple, semi-analytical model reproduces the peculiar propagation patterns. Hyperspectral imaging with a tunable narrowband laser further gives access to the polariton dispersion. The wide-field methodology holds high promise for in-depth and high-throughput studies of infrared nanophotonic structures.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a far-field nonlinear microscopy technique for imaging in-plane vector fields of propagating surface phonon polaritons.
motivation: Existing near-field microscopy mostly probes out-of-plane field components, but in-plane components are crucial for studying complex polariton modes like hyperbolic polaritons or skyrmions.
method: The authors use nonlinear infrared-visible wide-field sum-frequency generation microscopy with polarization-selective imaging to directly measure in-plane polariton field components.
result: They experimentally image surface phonon polaritons at the AlN-air interface and reproduce the propagation patterns with a semi-analytical model.
conclusion: The wide-field methodology enables high-throughput studies of infrared nanophotonic structures and provides direct access to in-plane polariton fields.

title: Higher-Order Vs. Quadratic Binary Optimization: Which Is Better For Probability Optimization With Tensor Sampling?
authors: Hadi Salloum (research Center Of The Artificial Intelligence Institute, Innopolis, University, Innopolis, Russia, Moscow Institute Of Physics And Technology, Moscow, Russia, Q Deep, Innopolis, Russia), Kirill Novoselov (research Center Of The Artificial Intelligence Institute, Innopolis, University, Innopolis, Russia), Aleksandr Pochtarev (research Center Of The Artificial Intelligence Institute, Innopolis, University, Innopolis, Russia), Yaroslav Kholodov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article explores the comparative strengths of Higher-Order Unconstrained Binary Optimization (HUBO) and Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) models in the context of probability optimization using tensor sampling techniques. HUBO can represent interactions beyond pairwise terms without introducing auxiliary variables, while QUBO benefits from a simpler algebraic structure and a wide range of established solvers. We combine a theoretical analysis of formulation expressiveness and reduction overhead with empirical experiments on synthetic polynomial objectives, RSA factorization, and Max-Cut instances. The results show that native HUBO formulations are often preferable when the original problem contains high-order interactions, because reducing such problems to QUBO increases the effective dimension seen by tensor samplers. At the same time, QUBO remains competitive for naturally quadratic problems. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting an optimization framework that balances model fidelity, dimension growth, and solver performance.
tldr: This paper compares HUBO and QUBO formulations for probability optimization using tensor sampling, focusing on computational performance rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To determine whether higher-order or quadratic binary optimization is more effective for probability optimization with tensor sampling, especially when high-order interactions are present.
method: Theoretical analysis of formulation expressiveness and reduction overhead, combined with empirical experiments on synthetic polynomial objectives, RSA factorization, and Max-Cut instances.
result: Native HUBO formulations are preferable for problems with high-order interactions, while QUBO remains competitive for naturally quadratic problems.
conclusion: The choice between HUBO and QUBO should balance model fidelity, dimension growth, and solver performance, providing practical guidance for optimization framework selection.

title: Sampling Using Hybrid Stochastic Dynamics
authors: Bj\"orn Engquist, Kui Ren, Yunan Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proposes a framework for sampling from the Gibbs distribution of a given potential using hybrid stochastic dynamics. In this framework, two distinct sampling dynamics are run in different regions of the state space. The two dynamics are coupled across the interface through natural transmission conditions that preserve the target distribution. Using a specially constructed regularization scheme, we establish an exponential rate of convergence for the hybrid dynamics to equilibrium. We also analyze the metastability properties of the hybrid dynamics in a radially symmetric landscape, showing that the hybrid scheme can improve the mean exit time. This advantage is further confirmed by the numerical experiments.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid stochastic dynamics framework for sampling from Gibbs distributions, combining two dynamics in different regions with coupling conditions to accelerate convergence.
motivation: Sampling from complex high-dimensional distributions is challenging; hybrid methods can improve efficiency by leveraging different dynamics in different regions.
method: Two distinct sampling dynamics are run in separate regions of state space and coupled via natural transmission conditions that preserve the target distribution, with a regularization scheme to ensure exponential convergence.
result: Exponential convergence to equilibrium is proven, and metastability analysis shows improved mean exit time in radially symmetric landscapes, confirmed by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The hybrid dynamics framework offers a principled way to combine sampling methods for better performance, particularly in metastable systems.

title: A Fast-Convergence Resolution Of The Stochastic Eigenproblem Using Halley's Method And The Spectral-Chaos Approach
authors: Hugo Esquivel, Kabir Oluwatobi Idowu, Guang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving stochastic eigenvalue problems has long been essential for informed decision-making, advancing scientific knowledge, and ensuring the reliability of engineering designs and applications. This paper underscores the need to continue enhancing existing numerical methods for solving the stochastic eigenproblem in order to improve convergence rates, computational efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we propose a novel spectral-chaos method for solving the stochastic (linear) eigenvalue problem, employing Halley's method as the root-finding algorithm to leverage its cubic convergence properties. Our method achieves maximal convergence in solving stochastic eigenvalue problems since its rate cannot be further improved using a higher-order Householder method due to the quadratic nature of the resulting system of equations. Additionally, due to the complexity of the resulting system of equations, a tensorial approach was developed to tackle the challenges associated with the dimensional multiplicity of the stochastic eigenvalue problem, without which the solution would have been intractable. The method is derived rigorously, with a detailed error analysis that highlights the benefit of using our approach when the eigenvector components are nearly known, the computational cost of the method is also rigorously presented, and an illustrative example is provided to demonstrate the implementation of the method. Subsequently, a case study is demoed to analyze the results and validate the advantages of using Halley's method over Newton's method and Monte Carlo simulations.
tldr: This paper proposes a spectral-chaos method using Halley's method to solve stochastic eigenvalue problems with cubic convergence.
motivation: Stochastic eigenvalue problems are important for decision-making and engineering reliability, but existing numerical methods need improved convergence and efficiency.
method: The authors combine spectral-chaos expansion with Halley's root-finding algorithm, and develop a tensorial approach to handle the high-dimensional stochastic system.
result: The method achieves maximal convergence (cubic) for the stochastic eigenproblem, outperforming Newton's method and Monte Carlo simulations in a case study.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a fast-converging and robust solution for stochastic eigenvalue problems, with potential applications in uncertainty quantification.

title: Deletion-Correcting Codes For The $\ell$-Symbol Read Channel
authors: Gennian Ge Zuo Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies deletion-correcting codes for the [MATH]-symbol read channel, whose noiseless output is the vector of all consecutive [MATH]-mers of a transmitted sequence. This model is motivated by overlapping-read mechanisms arising in nanopore sequencing, racetrack memories with consecutive read heads, and related sequence-labeling problems. We consider an adversarial setting in which a fixed number of [MATH]-mers are deleted from the read vector. Our first contribution is a structural characterization of the effect of such deletions: after a minimum number of [MATH]-mers are inserted to restore consistency, the resulting sequence is obtained from the transmitted sequence by deleting symbols from certain periodic substrings; when [MATH], these deletions correspond to complete minimum periods. Based on this characterization, we introduce check patterns and construct [MATH]-read deletion-correcting codes via power-sum syndromes. For every [MATH], we obtain single-deletion correcting codes with redundancy [MATH]. For [MATH], we construct [MATH]-ary [MATH]-read [MATH]-deletion correcting codes with redundancy [MATH], and for [MATH] with [MATH], we construct codes with redundancy [MATH]. We also study the sporadic parameter pairs [MATH] and obtain improved constructions, including binary [MATH]-read [MATH]-deletion correcting codes with redundancy [MATH] for [MATH], a non-binary [MATH]-read [MATH]-deletion correcting code with redundancy [MATH], a binary [MATH]-read [MATH]-deletion correcting code with redundancy [MATH], and a non-binary [MATH]-read [MATH]-deletion correcting code with redundancy [MATH].
tldr: This paper constructs deletion-correcting codes for the ℓ-symbol read channel, motivated by nanopore sequencing and racetrack memories.
motivation: Overlapping-read mechanisms in nanopore sequencing and racetrack memories require codes that correct deletions of ℓ-mers from the read vector.
method: The authors characterize the effect of ℓ-mer deletions via periodic substrings and construct codes using check patterns and power-sum syndromes.
result: They provide single-deletion correcting codes with redundancy log n + O(1) and multiple-deletion codes with redundancy O(ℓ log n) for various parameters.
conclusion: The proposed codes achieve near-optimal redundancy for the ℓ-symbol read deletion channel.

title: A Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem In Random And Simultaneous Dynamics
authors: Shrihari Sridharan Thirupathi Perumal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this manuscript, we consider finitely many maps defined on a compact probability space; each of which preserves the probability measure. We consider two aspects of growth of dynamical systems in this scenario; the first setting where we let some infinite lettered word determine the path through which the orbit of points evolve, while the second setting where we consider all possible paths through which the orbit of a set may evolve. Our aim in this paper is to provide a full description of the celebrated multiplicative ergodic theorem, originally due to Oseledets, for such dynamical systems that is point-valued (as in the first case) and set-valued (as in the second case).
tldr: This paper extends the multiplicative ergodic theorem to random and simultaneous dynamics on compact probability spaces.
motivation: To generalize Oseledets' theorem to settings where the dynamics are governed by random words or all possible paths.
method: The authors consider finitely many measure-preserving maps and analyze two scenarios: one with an infinite-letter word determining the orbit, and another considering all possible paths.
result: They provide a full description of the multiplicative ergodic theorem for both point-valued and set-valued dynamical systems.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous ergodic theory framework for random and simultaneous dynamics, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Adaptive Randomized Pivoting For Tensor Singular Value Decomposition Model
authors: Ahmadsho Akdodshoev, Valentin Leplat, Salman Ahmadi-Asl
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies how adaptive randomized pivoting (ARP), recently introduced for matrix column subset selection, can be extended to tensors in the t-product framework. We propose two constructions. The first one, called ARP-T-CUR, applies matrix ARP independently to the frontal slices of the tensor in the Fourier domain. This gives a Fourier-slicewise CUR approximation and leads to a direct expected-error bound inherited from the matrix theory. The second construction, called T-ARP, selects common lateral and horizontal slices for the whole tensor. This produces a genuine tensor cross approximation in the t-product sense, but also introduces a new difficulty: the same pivot indices must be used across all Fourier slices. We make this coupling explicit and prove an expected-error bound under a frequency-alignment condition measuring how far the common tensor-level sampling rule is from the slice-wise ARP sampling rules. This condition recovers the usual [MATH]-type factor when the leverage-score distributions are aligned across frequencies. We also discuss the resulting tensor cross approximation and its connection with t-DEIM. Numerical experiments on synthetic tensors, images, and videos illustrate the behavior of the proposed methods and show the benefit of common-index tensor sampling over standard tensor cross baselines.
tldr: Extends adaptive randomized pivoting for matrix column subset selection to tensors in the t-product framework, proposing two tensor CUR approximations.
motivation: Tensor decompositions are useful for large-scale data analysis, but existing methods lack adaptive sampling strategies that leverage randomized pivoting for improved efficiency and error bounds.
method: Proposes ARP-T-CUR, which applies matrix ARP independently to Fourier-domain slices, and T-ARP, which selects common slices across all frequencies with a coupling condition.
result: Derives expected-error bounds for both methods; numerical experiments on synthetic data, images, and videos show benefits over standard tensor cross approximations.
conclusion: Adaptive randomized pivoting can be effectively extended to tensors, yielding improved approximation quality and theoretical guarantees under certain alignment conditions.

title: Tight Lower Bounds And Optimal Constructions Of Locally Repairable Convertible Codes In The Split Regime
authors: Weijun Fang Haoming Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Erasure codes are a key technique for achieving fault-tolerant storage in modern distributed storage systems. As storage systems evolve, their code parameters often need to be adjusted to accommodate changes in storage scale, reliability requirements, and disk failure rates. Such adaptation is performed through code conversion, where data encoded under an initial code are transformed into data encoded under a final code. Convertible codes are designed to carry out this transformation efficiently while preserving desirable properties of the underlying codes. In this work, we study conversions between systematic optimal-distance locally repairable codes (LRCs), focusing on the read-bandwidth cost in the global split regime. We concentrate on the parameter range \(g^I,g^F\le r\), where the numbers of initial and final global parity nodes do not exceed the local dimension. For this entire range, we derive read-bandwidth lower bounds for stable optimal-distance locally repairable convertible codes (LRCCs) via an information-theoretic approach, without imposing any linearity assumption on the initial and final codes or on the conversion procedure. We then develop constructions based on MDS array codes with prescribed repair properties. According to the relative sizes of \(g^I\) and \(g^F\), the construction is divided into the three cases \(g^F=g^I\), \(g^F>g^I\), and \(g^F<g^I\); in each case, it attains the corresponding lower bound. Hence we characterize the optimal read-bandwidth cost for stable optimal-distance LRCCs throughout the parameter range \(g^I,g^F\le r\).
tldr: This paper derives tight lower bounds and optimal constructions for locally repairable convertible codes in distributed storage systems.
motivation: Distributed storage systems need to adapt code parameters over time; convertible codes enable efficient transformation between codes while preserving local repairability.
method: The authors use an information-theoretic approach to derive read-bandwidth lower bounds for stable optimal-distance locally repairable convertible codes, and construct optimal codes using MDS array codes with prescribed repair properties.
result: They characterize the optimal read-bandwidth cost for the parameter range where initial and final global parity nodes do not exceed the local dimension, covering three cases of relative sizes of global parity nodes.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of optimal read-bandwidth for stable optimal-distance LRCCs in the split regime, with no linearity assumptions.

title: An Orthogonal Approximate Message Passing Framework For Multiuser Communications
authors: Burak \c{c}akmak, Hao Yan, Alexander Fengler, Giuseppe Caire, Lei Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the open problem of constructing a Bayes-optimal iterative signal recovery algorithm for linear-Gaussian communication systems with random precoding at the transmitters.Specifically, we consider the received signal model [MATH], where [MATH] is white Gaussian noise, [MATH] are discrete-time channel matrices -- modeling a wide class of generally time-varying and dispersive linear channels with possibly multiple antennas -- and the precoding matrices [MATH] are drawn independently from a right-unitarily invariant random matrix ensemble. We consider generic (coded) systems where the users' signals [MATH] follow general (non-factorizing) distributions. For this model, we introduce a novel orthogonal/vector approximate message passing (OAMP/VAMP)-type framework, including an algorithm and its high-dimensional (but finite-sample) analysis. From an algorithmic standpoint, the proposed method can be interpreted as an between Minka's expectation propagation (EP)--a widely used method in machine learning--and OAMP. Our main theoretical contribution is the explicit finite-sample analysis of the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we analyze the associated inference problem via a replica-symmetric (RS) ansatz by using a novel disorder-averaging technique. Both the (rigorous) high-dimensional analysis of the algorithm and the RS ansatz reveal the same decoupling principle, establishing that the proposed algorithm is asymptotically Bayes-optimal under the validity of the RS ansatz.
tldr: This paper develops an orthogonal approximate message passing framework for multiuser communications with random precoding, focusing on Bayes-optimal iterative signal recovery.
motivation: The authors aim to solve the open problem of constructing a Bayes-optimal iterative signal recovery algorithm for linear-Gaussian communication systems with random precoding.
method: They introduce an OAMP/VAMP-type framework that bridges expectation propagation and OAMP, and provide finite-sample analysis along with a replica-symmetric ansatz.
result: The algorithm is shown to be asymptotically Bayes-optimal under the replica-symmetric ansatz, with both rigorous analysis and RS ansatz revealing the same decoupling principle.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers a theoretically grounded and practically relevant algorithm for multiuser communications, though its connection to quantum information or thermodynamics is absent.

title: Accelerated Sampling Using SamAdams Variable Timesteps And Position-adaptive Langevin Dynamics
authors: Peter A. Whalley Benedict Leimkuhler
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce an accelerated Langevin-based sampling method that is based on two complementary devices: adaptive timestepping, which automatically shrinks the effective integration step in stiff regions of phase space using a relaxed stiffness monitor, and (PAL) dynamics, which concentrates friction along the local force direction while preserving the canonical distribution as the exact invariant measure. The resulting combined scheme (SA-PAL) is implemented in a palindromic integrator which requires only one force evaluation per iteration through suitable organisation of the integration steps and by exploiting the rank-one-plus-scalar structure of the PAL friction tensor. We test the method on various model problems: the Rosenbrock function, a thin entropic channel, the Mueller-Brown potential, and a Bayesian parameterisation problem with a sparsity-inducing shrinkage prior. On the Rosenbrock and Mueller-Brown potentials mixing rates are improved by 1.5-3 times compared to fixed stepsize integration. Efficiency gains of more than an order of magnitude are documented in the other examples.
tldr: This paper introduces an accelerated Langevin sampling method using adaptive timestepping and position-dependent friction, but it is a classical computational statistics method with no quantum or thermodynamic content.
motivation: To improve sampling efficiency in stiff or constrained systems where standard Langevin dynamics is slow.
method: Combines adaptive timestepping (SamAdams) with position-adaptive Langevin (PAL) dynamics that concentrates friction along the force direction, implemented in a palindromic integrator requiring one force evaluation per step.
result: Mixing rates improved by 1.5–3× on Rosenbrock and Mueller-Brown potentials, and over an order of magnitude on a thin entropic channel and Bayesian inference problem.
conclusion: The SA-PAL method offers significant speedups for classical sampling problems, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Graph Isomorphism And Representation Theory
authors: Jacob Urisman Joshua A. Grochow
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce an approach to distinguishing isomorphism types of graphs based on vector spaces of polynomials that are set-wise invariant under permutations ("separating modules," which are representations of the symmetric group), inspired by the Geometric Complexity Theory approach to separating complexity classes (Mulmuley & Sohoni, SIAM J. Comput., 2001). We characterize the power of this method for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs under several different complexity measures: - We show that separating modules of "support-degree" [MATH] (each monomial touches at most [MATH] vertices) are equivalent to the counts of [MATH]-vertex subgraphs. This is strictly weaker than [MATH]-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman (F\"urer, ICALP '01). - We show that separating modules of symmetric circuit size [MATH] are equivalent to [MATH]-WL. This generalizes and strengthens a result of Dawar & Wilsenach (CSL '18; ICALP '20; ACM Trans. Comput. Log., 2022; Theory Comput., 2025): they proved one direction of this equivalence for invariant polynomials; we generalize to separating modules and prove both directions. - When considering only the multiplicities of separating modules (as was proposed in GCT by Mulmuley & Sohoni, ibid., rather than the polynomials themselves), we show that two graphs are separated by multiplicities if and only if their automorphism groups have different cycle indices. The latter result is notable in the analogy with GCT, as it is the only result we are aware of in which the multiplicity approach to separating isomorphism types of objects has been given an "intrinsic" characterization in terms of the objects themselves. We use this to show that for graphs, multiplicity obstructions are stronger than occurrence obstructions. We also connect invariant polynomials to the Graph Reconstruction Conjectures and Forman's "invariants of finite type" (Adv. Math., 2004).
tldr: This paper uses representation theory and invariant polynomials to study graph isomorphism, with connections to Weisfeiler-Leman and Geometric Complexity Theory.
motivation: To develop algebraic methods for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, inspired by complexity theory separations.
method: Introduces separating modules (representations of symmetric groups) and analyzes their power under support-degree and circuit size measures.
result: Shows equivalence between separating modules of bounded support-degree and subgraph counts, and between symmetric circuit size and Weisfeiler-Leman; also characterizes multiplicity obstructions via cycle indices.
conclusion: Provides new algebraic characterizations of graph isomorphism tests, with implications for complexity theory and graph reconstruction.

title: MergeLLL: A Hierarchical Divide-and-Conquer Framework For LLL-Based Lattice Reduction
authors: Niharika Gauraha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice basis reduction algorithms have various applications in computational number theory and lattice-based cryptography, but their complexity increases rapidly with the dimension. Motivated by the divide-and-conquer strategy of merge sort and incorporating PotLLL-style deep insertions during recombination, MergeLLL is proposed. In this framework, a lattice basis is split into sub-bases, local reductions are performed independently, and the full basis is reconstructed through hierarchical merging. The approach is focused on improving local lattice structure first before global basis properties are refined, resulting in enhanced Gram-Schmidt orthogonality and numerical stability, while overall computational cost is reduced. The method is naturally parallelizable, allowing efficient multicore and distributed execution. It is shown that the reduction and merging steps preserve the lattice structure through unimodular transformations and achieve logarithmic parallel depth. In experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices, improvements over classical lattice reduction algorithms are demonstrated, including better orthogonality, a reduced number of expensive swap operations, and an improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.
tldr: A hierarchical divide-and-conquer framework for LLL-based lattice reduction, improving efficiency and quality for lattice-based cryptography.
motivation: Lattice reduction algorithms are computationally expensive for high dimensions; a divide-and-conquer approach can reduce complexity and improve parallelism.
method: Splits a lattice basis into sub-bases, performs local reductions independently, then merges hierarchically using PotLLL-style deep insertions.
result: Demonstrates improved Gram-Schmidt orthogonality, numerical stability, reduced swap operations, and better Hermite factor on subset-sum and NTRU lattices.
conclusion: The proposed MergeLLL framework offers a scalable, parallelizable alternative to classical lattice reduction with higher quality bases.

title: A $q$-ary Local Criterion For The Radius-One Limited Permutation Channel And Almost-Optimal Binary Block-Concatenation Codes
authors: Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy Noam Ben Shimon (yohananov)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The radius-one limited permutation channel [MATH] maps a transmitted word to any word obtained by an arbitrary set of pairwise disjoint adjacent transpositions. This is the [MATH] case of the [MATH]-limited permutation channel of Langberg et al., and is also the zero-error version of simultaneous adjacent-swap errors. We study zero-error block-concatenation codes for this channel. Our first contribution is a [MATH]-ary two-stage local criterion for certifying free block-concatenation codes. The criterion replaces the global all-length confusability problem by finitely many local checks between blocks: a same-length truncated-ball test and a second-stage prefix test for unequal lengths. In the binary case, it yields explicit block-concatenation codes of rates [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. The best construction improves the previous string-concatenation rate [MATH] and comes within [MATH] of the known upper bound [MATH]. Although the criterion is only sufficient, we prove that it is rate-complete: for every alphabet size [MATH], the supremum of [MATH]-ary block rates certified by the criterion is exactly the [MATH]-ary zero-error capacity [MATH]. Thus it imposes no asymptotic rate loss. We also give an exact product-automaton verifier which decides, for a fixed prefix-free binary block set, whether the induced finite-length codes are correcting for all lengths. Finally, motivated by feedback settings, we study error detection. We prove a [MATH]-ary pairing upper bound and give a [MATH]-ary local detecting criterion. In the binary case, we construct a detecting block-concatenation code of rate [MATH], compared with the upper bound [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies zero-error block-concatenation codes for the radius-one limited permutation channel, a classical coding theory problem.
motivation: To design efficient error-correcting codes for a specific channel model involving adjacent transpositions, with applications in data storage and communication.
method: Introduces a q-ary local criterion to certify block-concatenation codes, reducing global confusability to finite local checks, and provides explicit binary constructions.
result: Achieves binary block-concatenation codes with rates up to 0.791, improving previous bounds and coming within 0.009 of the known upper bound.
conclusion: The local criterion is rate-complete, meaning it asymptotically achieves the zero-error capacity, and the constructions are near-optimal.

tldr: This paper numerically studies inequality measures in kinetic wealth-exchange and earthquake models, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand inequality distributions in complex systems such as wealth exchange and earthquakes.
method: Numerical simulations of two kinetic wealth-exchange models and two earthquake models, computing various inequality measures.
result: Quantitative comparisons of inequality measures across the different models.
conclusion: The study provides insights into inequality patterns in complex systems but does not relate to quantum or thermodynamic information processing.

title: Second-order Modified Mean-field Theory For Textured Immobilized Magnetic Nanoparticles
authors: Elena V. Grokhotova, Jing Zhong, Alexey O. Ivanov, And Ekaterina A. Elfimova
abstract:

A second-order modified mean-field theory has been developed to predict the static magnetization and initial magnetic susceptibility of textured ensembles of immobilized interacting superparamagnetic nanoparticles with uniaxial anisotropy. The theory takes into account the orientational texture of t…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065420] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: Develops a second-order modified mean-field theory for magnetization of textured immobilized magnetic nanoparticles.
motivation: To accurately predict static magnetization and initial magnetic susceptibility of textured ensembles of immobilized superparamagnetic nanoparticles with uniaxial anisotropy.
method: Extends the modified mean-field theory to second order, incorporating orientational texture and interparticle interactions.
result: The theory provides improved predictions for magnetization curves and susceptibility compared to first-order theories.
conclusion: The second-order theory is a valuable tool for understanding magnetic properties of textured nanoparticle systems.

[Phys. Rev. E 113, L062203] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies stability of compact solitons in discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equations on multilattices, a topic in nonlinear wave systems.
motivation: Understanding stability of compact solitons is important for nonlinear wave dynamics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors derive a sharp stability criterion using analytical and numerical methods for the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger equation on multilattices.
result: They establish a criterion for stability of minimal compact soliton states.

title: ChronoCast: A Time-series Paradigm For Molecular Dynamics Simulation Using Equivariant Graph Neural Networks
authors: Yuxing Wang, Zhongwei Zhang, Shuang Lu, Shuyue Shan, Vitaly A. Kuzkin, Anton M. Krivtsov, And Jie Chen
abstract:
Author(s): Yuxing Wang, Zhongwei Zhang, Shuang Lu, Shuyue Shan, Vitaly A. Kuzkin, Anton M. Krivtsov, and Jie Chen

We propose a time-series paradigm named ChronoCast for molecular dynamics simulation using an advanced autoregressive Equivariant Graph Neural Network, which reformulates the conventionally time-consuming integration process into a forecasting task. This reformulation in turn offers a promising solu…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065305] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: ChronoCast uses an equivariant graph neural network to forecast molecular dynamics trajectories, replacing traditional numerical integration.
motivation: Molecular dynamics simulations are computationally expensive due to small time steps; a time-series forecasting approach can accelerate simulations.
method: An autoregressive equivariant graph neural network is trained on MD trajectory data to predict future atomic positions and velocities.
result: The model achieves accurate long-term predictions with significant speedup compared to conventional integrators.
conclusion: Machine learning can effectively surrogate MD integration, enabling faster simulations while preserving physical accuracy.

title: Algebraic To Exponential Decay Of Spatial Correlations In One-dimensional And Confined Hard-core Fluids: A Laplace-pole Analysis
authors: Ana M. Montero And Andrés Santos
abstract:
Author(s): Ana M. Montero and Andrés Santos

We derive the asymptotic behavior of the radial distribution function [MATH] for one-dimensional (1D) hard-rod systems and related quasi-one-dimensional geometries at high packing fractions using Laplace transform techniques and pole analysis. By identifying the poles and residues of the Laplace tra…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064133] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the asymptotic decay of spatial correlations in one-dimensional hard-rod fluids using Laplace transform pole analysis.
motivation: Understanding the decay of correlations in confined hard-core fluids is important for statistical mechanics of classical fluids.
method: The authors use Laplace transform techniques and pole analysis to derive the asymptotic behavior of the radial distribution function at high packing fractions.
result: They show that spatial correlations decay algebraically in strictly 1D systems but exponentially in quasi-1D confined geometries.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for correlation decay in hard-core fluids, relevant to classical statistical mechanics.

title: Tiling By Near Coincidence
authors: Meshy Ochana And Ron Lifshitz
abstract:
Author(s): Meshy Ochana and Ron Lifshitz

Moiré patterns of twisted and scaled bilayers have recently emerged as a fertile source of quasiperiodic order in two-dimensional materials. Inspired by these systems, we introduce the near-coincidence method for generating quasiperiodic tilings of the plane. The method is intuitive—admitting pairs …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023330] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: Introduces a near-coincidence method for generating quasiperiodic tilings inspired by moiré patterns in twisted bilayers.
motivation: Moiré patterns in twisted 2D materials exhibit quasiperiodic order; the authors aim to provide a systematic tiling method to model such structures.
method: The near-coincidence method generates quasiperiodic tilings by overlaying two periodic lattices with a slight mismatch in scale or rotation, then selecting tiles that nearly coincide.
result: The method produces a variety of quasiperiodic tilings, including those with 12-fold symmetry, and can be tuned by adjusting the lattice parameters.
conclusion: The near-coincidence method offers an intuitive and flexible way to generate quasiperiodic tilings relevant to moiré materials.

title: Experimental Observations Of Cluster Synchronization In A Biologically Inspired Neuronal Network Of Chaotic Electronic Oscillators
authors: Karan K. H. Manjunatha, Joakim Vianney Ngamsa Tegnitsap, Manyu Zhao, Lucia Valentina Gambuzza, Yafang Dong, Wei Zhang, Pedro Antonio Valdes-Sosa, Stefano Boccaletti, Mattia Frasca, And Ludovico Minati

A recently introduced spectral block method is employed to predict the formatio…
